Brat behavior discourse of the week 

@puptosa is publicly accusing his handler @themazrim of skipping his weekly bath. Odin is away so this is advanced, extra-credit brattiness. (It also reminds me of my pup Ruffus telling everyone I “abandon” him… even if I’m just going to the bathroom.)

What I actually love about this little social media “drama” is that it highlights two things bratty behavior gets right:

1. You don’t get to be this public, playful, and unthreatened unless the dynamic is secure. That level of teasing only works when the relationship underneath it is solid.
2. Good brats understand that you need rules in order to bend them. Brattiness lives inside a framework. You’ve gotta know the rules to break them.

It’s actually a beautiful exchange between people who care deeply for each other.

So am I on Team Tosa (give him a bath) or Team Odin (punish him)? Honestly… both. If it was me, Tosa would absolutely get a bath—but I hope he’s prepared for some very intentional submersion, intense breath work, and learning why brats don’t bite the hand that holds the leash.

So thrilled with the food & service, I highly recommend for all types of occasions!

The Funniest Podcast on the Planet 🌍 ‼️

Rodney Dangerfield, 1921 to 2004.

Rodney was born Jacob Cohen in 1921, a kid from Queens in a house that never quite felt steady. As a young man he tried stand up under the name Jack Roy, dragging his jokes from one cheap club to another while the audience stared back in silence. The crowds did not remember Jack Roy, and for a while it felt like they never would.

Rodney Dangerfield only appeared when Jacob Cohen finally gave up. After years of bombing on stage and hustling off stage, Jacob walked away from show business and sold aluminum siding just to pay the bills. The man who was obsessed with making people laugh spent his days knocking on doors, wondering if the dream he had as a kid was just a bad joke.

Rodney Dangerfield became the second chance. In middle age, when most people have already decided who they are, Jacob came back with a new name and a new character, the sweaty guy in the wrinkled suit who gets no respect. The voice, the red tie, the one liners that landed one after another, suddenly the nobody from Queens turned into one of the most recognizable faces in comedy.

Rodney did not just want to work clubs, he wanted a home. In 1969 Rodney Dangerfield opened Dangerfield’s on the Upper East Side so he could sleep in his own bed, see his kids, and still step on stage every night. That little room on First Avenue became a magnet for killers, Jerry Seinfeld, Jim Carrey, Chris Rock and many others, and the look of the club was so iconic that it ended up on screen in Joker.

Rodney Dangerfield is gone now, but the room he built is still here. The old Dangerfield’s space has been reborn as Rodney’s Comedy, with new lights, a new bar, a new stage, and somehow I got to help broker this place into its next life. When you watch this reel and see a packed show in that room, you are not just looking at another New York comedy club. You are sitting inside a story that started with Jacob Cohen, the kid from Queens who refused to stay the guy nobody remembered.
